title: Shemini: strange fire (Leviticus 10:1–2)
hookLine: Nadav and Avihu bring fire not commanded and die; commentators still ask why

cards: Yesterday ended in joy: the sanctuary working at last, Aaron blessing the people, fire from God consuming the offering, the whole camp shouting for joy.
Then, with almost no pause, the very next verse turns everything over. Today's story is a hard one. It's only two verses long, and it doesn't explain itself.
Readers have argued about it ever since. There's no solving it today, only looking at it honestly.

teach.b: Here it is: "And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took each of them his censer, and put fire therein, and laid incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them. And there came forth fire from before the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD."

Aaron's two oldest sons, on the day of their father's first service. The text uses the very words it used one verse earlier for the fire that consumed the offering: fire from before the LORD. What did they do wrong?
The only clue is fire which He had not commanded them. The rabbis offered many answers, and Rashi records two.

One sage says they made a ruling of their own in front of Moses, their teacher, instead of asking him. Another says they came in drunk, since a few verses later priests are forbidden wine before serving.
A midrash in Leviticus Rabbah lists still more.
And some later commentators read it almost the opposite way: the brothers weren't wicked at all, but so full of love for God that they rushed too close, like moths to a flame, and couldn't come back.
What these readings share, from the harshest to the most tender: the brothers acted on their own fire. Not God's command, not their teacher's word, not the careful plan these chapters have followed.
Passion, or pride, or love; it wasn't listening. And that's as far as honesty can go. The Torah doesn't say more, and it would be dishonest to pretend it does.

how: The death of Nadav and Avihu is read in the portion Shemini and again in the Torah reading for Yom Kippur morning, which opens 'after the death of the two sons of Aaron'.

o: a censer: the pan that held fire and incense
eighth: the day the sanctuary service began
strange: fire that was never commanded

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah clearly explains what the brothers did wrong
it only says the fire was not commanded. the reasons come from later readers.
some commentators read the brothers as full of love, not wickedness
they rushed too close to God and couldn't come back.
this happened on an ordinary day, long after the sanctuary opened
it happened on the eighth day, the day of Aaron's first service.

games.q: you're one of Aaron's sons. the fire has just come from God onto the altar, and the people are shouting for joy. you're overflowing with feeling. what do the brothers do?
o: wait for Moses to tell them what's next.
bring their own fire and incense, not commanded.
go out and bless the people.
games.why: they offered strange fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them, and fire came forth and devoured them. the Torah never fully says why.

practice: Let Nadav and Avihu's story rest in front of you without choosing an explanation, and if an urge comes to settle it, to decide it was deserved or unfair, let that be there too.
Then, gently, think of a time your own enthusiasm ran ahead of your listening, and what it cost, without judging it. Breathe slowly, and hold the question open.

wordCard.voice: Shemini. Eighth. The portion where the eighth day's joy is broken by strange fire, and the Torah leaves us asking why.

orig.note: Hebrew: strange fire, or foreign fire, from Leviticus 10:1.

carryVoice: Your line: zeal without listening. Some questions are meant to stay open. See you tomorrow.
